segments.title: Why historical research keeps producing new projects
segments.summary: Questions raised while answering one problem can become new projects, as the aircraft-carrier and naval-aviation research shows.
segments.body: Historical projects start with questions, and work on one question routinely produces more. A personal folder labeled "questions" collects ideas that arise during other research, sometimes a couple of dozen from a single inquiry. The doctoral research on aircraft carriers and naval aviation provides the example: tracing how aircraft, ships, and their technologies developed alongside one another exposed further subjects to investigate. Each focused investigation can therefore reveal connections that become new projects.
segments.question: Why do historians never seem to run out of projects?
segments.answerShort: Because historical projects begin with questions, and answering one question usually produces many more.

evidence.note: He explains that research questions multiply and gives his carrier and naval aviation doctorate as an example.

segments.title: How a destroyer question became a Royal Navy study
segments.summary: Imprecise naming and thin coverage of destroyers led to a study of Royal Navy fleet destroyer development.
segments.body: Work on naval aviation exposed a separate problem with destroyers: historical accounts often named them imprecisely and gave too little attention to how they developed. The subject appeared deep enough to deserve the same level of research as aircraft carriers. Further work became Tribals, Battles and Darings, a study of the Royal Navy's large fleet destroyers and general-purpose destroyers across the 1930s, 1940s, and 1950s. The example shows how a gap in existing accounts can turn a side question into a substantial research project. It also connects changing ship classifications with design development and fleet roles.

evidence.note: He describes the destroyer research that became a study of Tribals, Battles, Darings, and Royal Navy destroyer development.

segments.title: Why historians keep longer lists of questions than answers
segments.summary: Research and teaching keep generating questions, so historians must remain students while sharing what they learn.
segments.body: The destroyer study produced about two sides of A4 filled with further questions. Some supplied research for videos, some are being addressed in books, and others remain for future projects. New work and newly encountered documents generate still more questions, making continued inquiry part of historical practice. Sharing knowledge and teaching belong to the same process because a good teacher must remain a student. The closing observation is that an academic historian's list of questions may be larger than the list of answers.

evidence.note: He links new research and documents to further questions, then connects historical practice with teaching and continued learning.
